title: 〜まで (even)
meaning: Gives an extreme or unexpected example: “even ...”. It implies that everything else is included too, of course.

senses.label: Extreme example
senses.meaning: Picks the least likely example: “even ...”. The hidden message is “so of course everything else, too”. Often used for things that surprise the speaker.
senses.connection: Noun + まで (「が」 and 「を」 are usually dropped); often used with 「〜てしまう」 or 「〜とは」
examples: Even little kids laughed at me.
Even my best friend doubts me.
Even that gentle teacher got angry.

senses.label: Adding one more thing
senses.meaning: Adds one more item on top of what is already there: “even ... too”. Often paired with 「〜だけでなく」, 「〜うえに」, or 「〜し」. It stresses that things keep getting worse (or better).
senses.connection: 〜だけでなく／〜うえに、Noun + まで
examples: Not only is it raining, but now there's thunder too.
I got lost, and on top of that I even lost my wallet.
They treated me to a meal, and even gave me a gift.

senses.label: After another particle
senses.meaning: Can follow particles like 「に」, 「から」, or 「で」, as in 「にまで」 or 「からまで」. Shows that an effect reaches an unexpected place or person.
senses.connection: Noun + に／から／で／と + まで
examples: That rumor even spread overseas.
I even get emails from people I don't know.

notes: The basic meaning of 「まで」 is “until / as far as” (an end point). This use extends that idea: the range stretches all the way to the most extreme case.
With a subject, 「〜までが」 is also possible and sounds stronger: 「子どもまでが知っている」.
「〜までに」 means “by (a deadline)” and has nothing to do with this use.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: When bad luck keeps coming, 「まで」 stresses that things keep getting worse.
daily.example: The train was late, and someone even stole my umbrella.

daily.title: Thanking a friend
daily.description: Visiting a friend who prepared everything with care, you express happy surprise.
daily.example: You even made a cake for me yourself?

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: When news reports a disaster spreading, 「にまで」 is common.
daily.example: The damage even reached the neighboring town.

work.title: Reporting a growing problem
work.description: Telling your boss a problem has affected people you didn't expect, such as clients.
work.example: This trouble even caused inconvenience to our business partners.

work.title: Thanking a client
work.description: Thanking someone for paying attention to every detail.
work.example: Thank you for considering even the smallest details.

etymology: 「まで」 is an old particle marking the end of a range (“up to ...”). From “all the way to the farthest end” came the sense “even the extreme case is included”, meaning “even”. Its earlier origin is debated.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: 「さえ」 stresses “not even the most basic thing”, usually with negative content: 「水さえ飲めない」. 「まで」 stresses that the range has spread somewhere unexpected, often when adding something: 「雷まで鳴り出した」.

similar.title: 〜だって (even / also)
similar.explanation: 「だって」 is casual and means “even ... is no exception”. 「まで」 means “this got added too”, with a sense of surprise.

similar.title: 〜まで (end point)
similar.explanation: The 「まで」 in 「駅まで歩く」 marks an end point in space or time. That is the original meaning; “even” grew out of it.

title: 〜だって (even / also)
meaning: Casual speech, similar to 「でも」 or 「も」. Means “even ...” or “any ... at all”, stressing that there are no exceptions.

senses.label: Even ...
senses.meaning: Gives one example and says even that is no exception, so everything else is too. Similar to 「〜でも」 or 「〜も」, but more casual and more emphatic than 「でも」.
senses.connection: Noun + だって
examples: Even a child knows something like that.
Even teachers make mistakes sometimes.
I wanted to go too, you know!

senses.label: Question word + だって
senses.meaning: After a question word, it means “any ... at all” (who-, when-, what-ever). Same as 「〜でも」.
senses.connection: 誰／いつ／どこ／何 + だって
examples: Anyone can do something like that.
I'm always on your side.
I'm not picky, so I can eat anything.

senses.label: Listing examples
senses.meaning: 「AだってBだって」 lists two or more examples: “whether it's A or B, ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + だって + Noun + だって
examples: Meat or fish, I like everything.
Phone or email, contact me anytime.

notes: This is casual. In formal situations or writing, use 「でも」 or 「も」.
「だって」 at the start of a sentence means “but / because” and is used for excuses. That is a conjunction, not this pattern.
「〜んだって」 is hearsay (“I heard ...”), and 「読んだって」「泳いだって」 are 「〜たって」 (“even if ...”). Both are different from this pattern.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: When a friend lacks confidence, tell them anyone can do it.
daily.example: Don't worry. With practice, anyone can learn to do it.

daily.title: Feeling treated unfairly
daily.description: When family or friends criticize you, stress that you have your own problems too.
daily.example: I'm busy too, you know!

daily.title: Getting a child to eat
daily.description: A parent talking to a picky eater.
daily.example: You have to eat your vegetables too.

work.title: Chatting with a close coworker
work.description: Comforting a coworker who made a mistake. In formal settings, switch to 「でも」.
work.example: Even veterans make mistakes.

etymology: Usually explained as the copula 「だ」 + the classical particle 「とて」 (「って」 in speech), i.e. a casual form of 「だとて」. It originally meant something like “even if you say it's ...”, and later came to work like the particle 「でも」.

similar.title: 〜でも (question word + でも)
similar.explanation: 「誰でも」「いつでも」 mean the same as 「誰だって」「いつだって」. 「でも」 is neutral and fine in formal settings; 「だって」 is casual and more emphatic.

similar.title: 〜まで (even)
similar.explanation: 「まで」 carries surprise: “even this got added”. 「だって」 stresses “this is no exception either”.

similar.title: 〜たって
similar.explanation: 「〜たって」 follows verbs and adjectives and means “even if ...”. With voicing it becomes 「〜だって」 (「読んだって」). The pattern here follows nouns and question words.

meaning: Says that meeting one condition is enough and nothing else matters. Like “as long as ...” or “if only ...”.
connection: Noun + さえ + 〜ば; verb ます-stem + さえ + すれば; verb te-form + さえ + いれば

senses.label: Noun + さえ〜ば
senses.meaning: 「さえ」 marks the only condition needed, followed by a ば-form. It stresses “as long as I have this, it's fine”. The most common forms are 「〜さえあれば」 and 「〜さえよければ」.
senses.connection: Noun + さえ + あれば／なければ／よければ／verb ば-form
examples: If only I had the time, I'd travel more.
As long as the weather is good, you can see Mt. Fuji from the summit.
If it's okay with you, shall we meet tomorrow?

senses.label: Verb + さえすれば
senses.meaning: When the condition is an action, use 「ます-stem + さえすれば」: “as long as you just do ...”. For する-verbs, use 「〜さえすれば」 or 「〜しさえすれば」.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + さえ + すれば
examples: As long as you take this medicine, you'll get better quickly.
As long as you practice every day, you'll improve.
I think as long as you apologize, you'll be forgiven.

senses.label: Condition about a state
senses.meaning: 「te-form + さえいれば」 means “as long as a state continues”. い-adjectives use 「く + さえあれば」; nouns and な-adjectives use 「で + さえあれば」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + さえ + いれば; い-adjective く + さえ + あれば; noun／な-adjective で + さえ + あれば
examples: As long as you follow the rules, there's no problem.
As long as my family is healthy, that's enough.
As long as it's cheap, any store is fine.

notes: The second half usually shows a positive result, like “it will work” or “no problem”.
Where 「さえ」 goes depends on the condition: after a noun, after the ます-stem (「飲みさえすれば」), or after the te-form (「守ってさえいれば」). 「飲むさえすれば」 is wrong.
In speech, 「〜さえ〜たら」 and 「〜さえ〜なら」 are also used: 「君さえよかったら」.
「さえ」 on its own (“not even”) usually goes with negatives and is different from this pattern.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: Cheering up a friend who is nervous before an exam.
daily.example: As long as you review properly, you'll pass.

daily.title: Inviting someone politely
daily.description: When inviting a friend, first consider their schedule.
daily.example: If it's okay with you, want to go out together this weekend?

daily.title: Talking about life
daily.description: Describing how easily you are satisfied.
daily.example: As long as I have good food, I'm happy.

work.title: Training a new employee
work.description: A senior tells a newcomer that following the procedure prevents big mistakes.
work.example: As long as you follow the manual, you won't make any big mistakes.

work.title: Business visit request
work.description: Telling a client you'd like to visit if it suits them.
work.example: If it's convenient for you, I'd like to visit next week.

etymology: 「さえ」 is thought to come from the old word 「添へ（そへ）」, “to add”. From “adding one more” came “even”. Combined with the conditional 「ば」, it means “adding just this one condition is enough”.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: 「さえ」 alone means “even”, usually with negatives: 「名前さえ書けない」. 「〜さえ〜ば」 means “as long as ...” and is a conditional.

similar.title: 〜ば (conditional)
similar.explanation: 「〜ば」 alone is a general condition. Adding 「さえ」 stresses “this is the only condition needed; nothing else matters”.

similar.title: 〜だけで
similar.explanation: 「〜だけで」 means “just by ...”, focusing on how little is needed: 「見るだけで楽しい」. 「〜さえ〜ば」 focuses on “meeting this condition is enough” and is hypothetical.

meaning: Lists two things of the same kind or a matching pair: “both ... and ...”, or “there are ... and there are ...”.
connection: Noun + も + verb／adjective ば-form、noun + も + 〜

senses.label: Both ... and ...
senses.meaning: Gives two facts pointing the same way: “both ... and ...”. They can be two good points or two bad points. It stresses “not just one”.
senses.connection: Noun + も + verb ば-form／adjective ければ、noun + も + similar predicate
examples: He sings, and he dances too.
This room gets lots of sun, and it's close to the station.
My older brother cooks and cleans.

senses.label: Some ..., some ...
senses.meaning: Gives two opposite things: “there are times when ... and times when ...”. 「AもあればBもある」 and 「AもいればBもいる」 describe how something has many sides.
senses.connection: Noun + も + あれば／いれば、noun + も + ある／いる
examples: Life has its good times and its bad times.
Some people agree, and some people disagree.

senses.label: Neither ... nor ...
senses.meaning: With a negative, 「AもなければBもない」 means “there is neither A nor B”. Often expresses dissatisfaction or resignation.
senses.connection: Noun + も + なければ、noun + も + ない
examples: I have neither money nor time.
This town has neither a movie theater nor a bookstore.

notes: The two items must point the same way (both good or both bad), or form a matching contrast. You can't combine just anything.
Here 「ば」 does not mean “if”. It shows that two things exist side by side.
It has more rhythm than 「〜し、〜も」 and is used in both writing and speech.
The N1 pattern 「〜も〜なら〜も」 criticizes both sides (“both are equally bad”). Don't mix them up.

daily.title: Talking about your family
daily.description: Proudly telling a friend how capable your father is.
daily.example: My dad cooks, and he does the laundry too.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Helping a friend who had a setback to look at the bigger picture.
daily.example: Life has fun times and hard times.

daily.title: Complaining about your neighborhood
daily.description: Telling a friend how inconvenient your area is.
daily.example: Around here, there's neither a convenience store nor a bus stop.

work.title: Recommending a colleague
work.description: Listing a coworker's skills when recommending her to your boss.
work.example: She can do English, and she speaks Chinese too.

work.title: Summing up a meeting
work.description: Explaining that opinions about a proposal are divided.
work.example: Some people support this plan, and some are against it.

etymology: A combination of 「も」 (“also”, for things of the same kind) and the ば-form. 「AもすればBもする」 originally meant “since there is A, there is also B”. Here 「ば」 shows coexistence, not a condition.

similar.title: 〜し
similar.explanation: 「〜し〜し」 also lists and adds things, more loosely, and can hint at reasons. 「〜も〜ば〜も」 stresses that two things go together as a pair and has a stronger rhythm.

similar.title: 〜も〜なら〜も
similar.explanation: 「親も親なら子も子だ」 says both sides are bad, with strong criticism. 「〜も〜ば〜も」 itself is a neutral list.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: 「AばかりでなくB」 means “not only A but also B”, with the focus on B. In 「〜も〜ば〜も」, both items carry equal weight.

title: 〜(number)は (at least)
meaning: After a number or amount, shows the minimum the speaker estimates or demands: “at least ...”.

senses.label: Minimum estimate
senses.meaning: Gives a lowest estimate of an amount: “at least ...”, “no less than ...”. Often used with 「少なくとも」 or 「最低」, and with endings like 「〜だろう」 or 「〜かかる」.
senses.connection: Number + は + かかる／ある／する, etc.
examples: It takes at least 30 minutes to walk to the station.
This bag probably weighs at least 10 kilos.
I want at least three days off.

senses.label: Minimum goal / habit
senses.meaning: Means “at least this much should be done”, showing the speaker's demand, intention, or habit.
senses.connection: Number + は + verb (〜たい／〜ている／〜たほうがいい, etc.)
examples: I study at least two hours every day.
You should sleep at least eight hours a day.
I want to climb Mt. Fuji at least once.

notes: Here 「は」 after a number is not a topic marker. It means “at least”.
It is often used with 「少なくとも」, 「せめて」, or 「最低」 to make the meaning clearer.
Number + 「も」 means “as many as ...”, the opposite direction: 「3時間もかかった」 (it took a whole three hours).

daily.title: Estimating time
daily.description: Answering a friend who asks how long it takes to the airport.
daily.example: It takes at least an hour from here to the airport.

daily.title: Talking about healthy habits
daily.description: Describing your exercise routine.
daily.example: I try to walk at least 10,000 steps every day.

daily.title: Recommending a movie
daily.description: Strongly recommending a movie to a friend.
daily.example: This movie is worth watching at least twice.

work.title: Estimating a schedule
work.description: Telling your boss the minimum time a task will need.
work.example: This work will take at least a week.

work.title: Explaining a budget
work.description: Stating a project's minimum budget in a meeting.
work.example: We need at least one million yen.

etymology: 「は」 is a particle for topics and contrast. After a number, it implies a contrast like “I can't say about anything else, but this much is certain”, which gives the meaning “at least”.

similar.title: 〜も (emphasizing amount)
similar.explanation: Number + 「も」 stresses that an amount is large, more than expected: 「10キロもある」 (it's a whole 10 kilos). Number + 「は」 gives a minimum estimate: 「10キロはある」 (it's at least 10 kilos).

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい
similar.explanation: 「30分くらい」 just means “about 30 minutes”. 「30分は」 means “at least 30 minutes, maybe more”.

title: 〜なんか・〜など (belittling)
meaning: Used to give a casual example, to look down on something, or to be modest about yourself. With a negative, it makes the denial stronger. 「なんか」 is casual; 「など」 is more formal.
connection: Noun (+ particle)／い-adjective く-form／verb te-form + なんか (など)

senses.label: Casual example
senses.meaning: Picks one example out of many, softening the tone: “... or something”, “how about ...?”. Often used for suggestions and recommendations.
senses.connection: Noun + なんか (+ どう？／いかが？／いい)
examples: How about some tea or something?
I think flowers like these would make a nice gift.
A dress like this one would probably suit you.

senses.label: Belittling / modesty
senses.meaning: Shows contempt or dislike for something, or modesty about yourself: “someone like ...”, “the likes of ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + なんか (+ に／と／で)
examples: I don't care about someone like him anymore.
That's really impossible for someone like me.
There's no way I'll lose to the likes of you!

senses.label: Stronger denial
senses.meaning: After an い-adjective く-form or a verb te-form, followed by a negative. Strongly denies what the other person said: “I'm not ... at all!”
senses.connection: い-adjective く-form + なんか + ない; verb te-form + なんか + いない
examples: I'm not scared at all!
I'm not crying!
I never said anything like that.

senses.label: Formal 「など」
senses.meaning: 「など」 is the written, formal version of 「なんか」. It can also show modesty, contempt, or a strong denial. Common in writing and formal settings.
senses.connection: Noun + など (+ ない／ません)
examples: Someone like me still has a lot to learn.
I have never heard of such a thing.
I am not lying.

notes: 「なんか」 at the start of a sentence or on its own means “somehow / kind of” (「なんか変だね」). That is an adverb, not this pattern.
Using 「〜なんか」 about other people can sound condescending; using it about yourself sounds modest.
「なんて」 can also belittle, but it is stronger and can also show surprise.
「〜や〜など」 is a neutral list with no belittling tone.

daily.title: Shopping with a friend
daily.description: Making a casual suggestion while shopping.
daily.example: How about this bag?

daily.title: Accepting a compliment modestly
daily.description: Answering humbly when someone praises you.
daily.example: Oh no, I've still got a long way to go.

daily.title: Stubbornly denying
daily.description: Denying it when a friend says “You're scared, aren't you?”
daily.example: I'm not scared or anything!

work.title: Suggesting an idea in a meeting
work.description: Politely offering one option for everyone to consider.
work.example: For example, how about a design like this?

work.title: Award speech
work.description: Formally and humbly saying you hardly deserve it, using 「など」.
work.example: I am honored that someone like me has received such an award.

etymology: 「なんか」 is usually said to come from 「何か（なにか）」, and 「など」 from 「何と（なにと）→なんど→など」. Both started as vague “... or something” and developed meanings of giving examples and belittling.

similar.title: 〜なんて
similar.explanation: Both can belittle. 「なんて」 is stronger and can also show surprise (「会えるなんて！」). 「なんか」 can soften a suggestion; 「なんて」 usually can't.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「AやBなど」 is an objective list with no feeling. 「なんか・など」 here carries softness, contempt, or modesty.

similar.title: 〜でも (giving an example)
similar.explanation: 「お茶でも飲みませんか」 also gives a casual example, usually in invitations. 「お茶なんかどう？」 is more casual and doesn't need an invitation form.

meaning: Casual. Shows surprise, disbelief, or contempt. Also replaces 「などと」 or 「という」 when quoting, and is a casual form of 「何と」.

senses.label: Surprise
senses.meaning: Shows that something is unexpected or hard to believe, or expresses strong feeling. Often ends the sentence as 「〜なんて」, or is followed by 「信じられない」 or 「思わなかった」.
senses.connection: Plain form + なんて (+ 信じられない／思わなかった)
examples: Fancy meeting you here!
I can't believe he failed the exam.
You're traveling abroad alone? That's amazing.

senses.label: Belittling / rejecting
senses.meaning: Shows contempt, dislike, or dismissal, more strongly than 「なんか」. About yourself, it sounds modest.
senses.connection: Noun + なんて
examples: I hate studying.
There's no way ghosts exist.
I've still got a long way to go.

senses.label: Quoting / naming
senses.meaning: Replaces 「などと」 or 「という」 to quote words or a name, with a tone of surprise or disapproval.
senses.connection: Quote + なんて + 言う／思う; noun + なんて + noun
examples: Don't say things like “I want to quit”.
I don't know anyone called Tanaka.
I never imagined we would lose.

senses.label: Casual 「何と」
senses.meaning: Also the casual form of 「何と」. Used in questions (“how / what”) or at the start of a sentence for “What a ...!”
senses.connection: なんて + 言う／読む; なんて + adjective + のだろう
examples: How do you read this kanji?
What a beautiful view!

notes: Both 「なんて」 and 「なんか」 can belittle, but 「なんて」 is stronger and can also show surprise.
「なんて」 can sound rude to superiors or in formal settings. The formal options are 「など」, 「などと」, and 「とは」.
When showing surprise, the rest of the sentence is often dropped, leaving just 「〜なんて」.

daily.title: Hearing good news
daily.description: Telling your family excitedly that you won the lottery.
daily.example: I can't believe I won the lottery. It's like a dream!

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Stopping a friend who is putting themselves down.
daily.example: Don't say you're no good.

daily.title: Asking how to read something
daily.description: Asking someone about a kanji you don't know.
daily.example: How do you read this?

work.title: Hearing surprising news
work.description: Privately expressing surprise that a coworker is quitting.
work.example: I had no idea Tanaka-san was leaving the company.

etymology: One theory says it comes from 「などと」, another from 「何と（なにと）」; in modern speech the two have merged. The belittling and quoting uses relate to 「などと」, while the question and exclamation uses come from 「何と」.

similar.title: 〜なんか・〜など (belittling)
similar.explanation: Both can belittle. 「なんか」 can also give soft examples; 「なんて」 is stronger and has the surprised “I can't believe ...” use.

similar.title: 〜とは (surprise)
similar.explanation: 「〜とは」 also shows surprise, but it is written style. 「〜なんて」 is spoken.

similar.title: 〜なんという／なんと〜 (exclamation)
similar.explanation: Sentence-initial 「なんて」 for exclamations equals 「なんと」, which is more formal and written.

meaning: Gives one example while implying that something similar would also do: “... or something”.
connection: Noun／plain form + か何か (casual: かなんか)

senses.label: Example of a kind
senses.meaning: Uses one example to stand for a whole type, meaning “not only this; something similar is fine too”. Common in suggestions and requests.
senses.connection: Noun + か何か
examples: Shall we have coffee or something?
Please lend me a pen or something to write with.
Let's go see a movie or something this weekend.

senses.label: Guess / uncertainty
senses.meaning: The speaker isn't sure and can only guess roughly: “probably ... or something”. Often used with 「らしい」, 「みたい」, or 「かな」.
senses.connection: Noun／plain form + か何か + らしい／みたいだ／だろう
examples: Apparently they're off with a cold or something.
Looks like there was an accident or something outside.
Is that person an actor or something?

notes: In casual speech, 「かなんか」 is common: 「ジュースかなんか買ってくる」.
It is more casual than 「〜など」 and stresses “it doesn't have to be exactly this”.
In 「誰か何か言った？」, 「誰か」 and 「何か」 are separate words: “Did someone say something?” That is not this pattern.

daily.title: Inviting a friend
daily.description: Asking a friend to go out and relax somewhere.
daily.example: If you're free, want to get tea or something?

daily.title: Guessing why a friend is late
daily.description: Guessing with others why a friend still hasn't come.
daily.example: Didn't Tanaka oversleep again or something?

daily.title: Asking family for something
daily.description: Your hands are wet and you ask for something to dry them.
daily.example: Is there a towel or something?

work.title: Preparing for a meeting
work.description: Asking a coworker to prepare some drinks.
work.example: Please have some tea or something ready before the meeting.

work.title: Looking after a client
work.description: Offering a waiting client a magazine or the like.
work.example: Shall I bring you a magazine or something while you wait?

etymology: A combination of 「か」 (“or”) and the indefinite 「何か」 (“something”). Literally “... or something”.

similar.title: 〜なんか・〜など (belittling)
similar.explanation: 「お茶なんかどう？」 also gives an example, but 「なんか」 can belittle. 「か何か」 just leaves it open: “something else is fine too”.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「AやBなど」 lists several known items. 「Aか何か」 names only one; the rest is unclear.

similar.title: 〜とか〜とか
similar.explanation: 「〜とか」 is casual and can give two or more examples. 「〜か何か」 usually gives just one.

title: 〜とか (hearsay)
meaning: Reports something heard but not certain: “I heard ... or something”. Vaguer than 「そうだ」.
connection: Plain form (noun／な-adjective + だ) + とか

senses.label: Hearsay at sentence end
senses.meaning: Placed at the end to pass on news you heard, while showing you're not completely sure: “I heard that apparently ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + とか。
examples: I heard Tanaka-san is getting married next month.
I heard the department manager is on a business trip today.
I heard a famous writer used to come to this shop.

senses.label: Hearsay reason
senses.meaning: 「〜とかで」 gives a reason you heard: “saying that ...”, “apparently because ...”. The next clause gives the result.
senses.connection: Plain form + とかで、〜
examples: She's off today; apparently she caught a cold.
The bus is late; something about road work.

senses.label: Vague quote
senses.meaning: 「〜とか言う」 or 「〜とかいう」 quotes someone's words or a name vaguely, showing you don't remember exactly.
senses.connection: Plain form／noun + とか + 言う／いう
examples: He said something about rain tomorrow.
You got a call from someone called Yamada or something.

notes: It is vaguer and more casual than 「〜そうだ」 or 「〜らしい」, and common in small talk.
The listing 「〜とか〜とか」 follows nouns and usually appears twice. Hearsay 「とか」 usually comes at the end of a sentence or as 「とかで」.
Avoid it in formal reports. Use 「〜とのことです」 or 「〜そうです」 instead.

daily.title: Chatting with a neighbor
daily.description: Sharing news about a family nearby.
daily.example: I heard the daughter next door is going abroad to study next year.

daily.title: Passing on why someone left
daily.description: Telling a friend why someone went home early.
daily.example: Sato-san went home; something about a fever.

daily.title: Chatting after the news
daily.description: Talking about what the weather forecast said.
daily.example: I heard this summer is going to be record-breakingly hot.

work.title: Passing on news to a coworker
work.description: Telling a coworker informally about the boss.
work.example: The section chief said something about being late today because of something urgent.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 and 「か」, which shows uncertainty. Literally “they say ..., maybe”, which gives the tone of “I heard, but I'm not sure”.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: 「そうだ」 clearly says the information comes from elsewhere and is more objective. 「とか」 is vaguer, hinting “I'm not so sure myself”.

similar.title: 〜とか〜とか
similar.explanation: The listing use follows nouns to give examples: 「パンとかご飯とか」. The hearsay use follows a sentence, usually at the end.

similar.title: 〜んだって
similar.explanation: 「んだって」 is also casual hearsay, but sounds more certain and friendlier. 「とか」 has a fuzzy “seems like it” feel.

title: 〜って (quote / topic)
meaning: In casual speech, replaces 「と」, 「という」, 「は」, or 「そうだ」. Used to quote, pass on hearsay, bring up a topic, or introduce a name.

senses.label: Quoting
senses.meaning: Replaces the quoting particle 「と」 before 「言う」, 「思う」, 「聞く」, etc. Very common in speech.
senses.connection: Plain form + って + 言う／思う／聞く
examples: He said he's taking tomorrow off.
I was relieved to hear it's all fine now.
I don't think she's coming.

senses.label: Hearsay at sentence end
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence it passes on what you heard, like 「そうだ」. With rising intonation, it checks: “I heard ..., is that true?”
senses.connection: Plain form + って。／って？
examples: Tanaka-san is moving next week, I heard.
They say it'll rain tomorrow.
I heard the exam was postponed. Is that right?

senses.label: Topic
senses.meaning: Brings up a topic and then comments on it or defines it, like 「は」, 「とは」, or 「というのは」. Often with feeling or a question.
senses.connection: Noun／plain form + って + comment／definition
examples: Japanese is hard, isn't it?
Is life in Tokyo fun?
What is love, anyway?

senses.label: Names
senses.meaning: 「〜っていう + noun」 is like 「という」 and introduces a name.
senses.connection: Noun + っていう + noun
examples: You got a call from someone named Suzuki.
Do you know a shop called “Sakura”?

notes: Very casual. In formal writing, use 「と」, 「という」, 「は」, or 「そうだ」 as appropriate.
The 「って」 in te-forms like 「言って」 or 「持って」 is part of the verb ending, not this pattern.
At the end of a sentence, 「って」 is usually hearsay; in the middle, followed by a comment, it's usually a topic. Position and intonation tell them apart.

daily.title: Passing on a family message
daily.description: A child tells the family dinner is ready.
daily.example: Mom says dinner's ready.

daily.title: Chatting with a friend
daily.description: Talking about an app you use a lot lately.
daily.example: This app is really handy, isn't it?

daily.title: Asking about someone
daily.description: Asking a friend if they know a certain person.
daily.example: Hey, do you know Yamada-san?

work.title: Passing on news to a coworker
work.description: Telling a coworker the boss's plans informally.
work.example: The department manager says the meeting starts at three.

etymology: Usually explained as a casual contraction of 「と言って」, 「という」, etc. The quoting particle 「と」 gained a small っ and became 「って」.

similar.title: 〜って (quote / topic) N4
similar.explanation: Its basic uses (quoting and topic) are learned at N4. Here, hearsay and naming are added, and the differences between the uses are sorted out.

similar.title: 〜んだって
similar.explanation: 「〜んだって」 is 「のだ」 + 「って」 and is used only for passing on hearsay, with an “explaining the situation” feel.

similar.title: 〜というのは
similar.explanation: The topic/definition 「って」 is the casual form of 「というのは」, which is more formal.

meaning: Casual. Passes on news you heard from someone else: “I heard ...”.
connection: Verb／い-adjective plain form + んだって; noun／な-adjective + なんだって

senses.label: Passing on hearsay
senses.meaning: Tells the listener news you heard. More casual and friendly than 「〜そうだ」, mostly used with friends and family.
senses.connection: Plain form + んだって; noun／な-adjective + なんだって
examples: I heard Yamada-san is getting married next month.
I heard that restaurant is really good.
I heard it's going to rain tomorrow.

senses.label: Checking hearsay
senses.meaning: With rising intonation, checks with the listener whether what you heard is true: “I heard ..., is that true?”
senses.connection: Plain form + んだって？
examples: I heard you're quitting your job?
I heard you won the lottery? Really?

senses.label: 「んですって」
senses.meaning: 「〜んですって」 is more polite and was traditionally used more by women. It is also used to ask back in surprise.
senses.connection: Plain form + んですって
examples: I heard the people next door are moving out next month.
Oh my, you're leaving already?

notes: Use it only with people you're close to. With superiors or in formal settings, use 「〜そうです」.
Nouns and な-adjectives need 「な」: 「雨なんだって」, not 「雨だんだって」.
The 「だって」 in 「読んだって」 or 「死んだって」 is the voiced form of 「〜たって」 (“even if ...”) and leads into another clause. It is not hearsay.

daily.title: Sharing gossip
daily.description: Sharing news you heard with a friend.
daily.example: Hey, I heard Sato-san and Suzuki-san are dating.

daily.title: Passing on the weather
daily.description: Telling your family about tomorrow's weather.
daily.example: I heard a typhoon is coming tomorrow.

daily.title: Checking news
daily.description: Checking directly with a friend you heard is studying abroad.
daily.example: I heard you're going abroad to study? That's great.

work.title: Chatting with a coworker
work.description: Talking about personnel changes with a close coworker at lunch.
work.example: I heard a new department manager is coming next month.

etymology: Made of 「んだ」, the casual form of explanatory 「のだ」, plus the quoting 「って」. It originally meant “(someone) says that ...”.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: 「そうだ」 works in formal settings and writing. 「んだって」 is only for close relationships and sounds friendlier.

similar.title: 〜って (quote / topic)
similar.explanation: Sentence-final 「〜って」 can also show hearsay: 「来週引っ越すって」. Adding 「んだ」 gives an “explaining the situation” tone.

similar.title: 〜とか (hearsay)
similar.explanation: 「とか」 is uncertain, vague hearsay. 「んだって」 sounds more certain.

meaning: Casual. Brings up a person as a topic with a tone of annoyance, resignation, or affection. Also used to urge someone impatiently or insist on something.
connection: Noun (person) + ったら; verb te-form／〜なさい／dictionary form + ったら

senses.label: Bringing up a person
senses.meaning: Mentions someone close and then their problem, with a “what am I going to do with them” feeling of annoyance, resignation, or affection. Can also be used about yourself. Like “Honestly, ...” or “Oh, that ...”.
senses.connection: Noun (person) + ったら (often after 「さん」, 「ちゃん」, family terms, or 「私」)
examples: Honestly, Mom forgot her phone again.
My kid doesn't study at all.
Silly me, I forgot my keys again.

senses.label: Urging / insisting
senses.meaning: Follows an order, request, or your own claim, repeating it impatiently because the other person isn't listening: “I told you ...!” 「〜ってば」 is also used.
senses.connection: Verb te-form／〜なさい + ったら; dictionary form + ったら + dictionary form
examples: I said get up already!
I said stop it!
I said I'm going, so I'm going!

notes: Use it only with people you're close to. With superiors it sounds rude.
The 「ったら」 in 「行ったら」 or 「言ったら」 is the conditional 〜たら, not this pattern.
When urging, it can be swapped with 「〜ってば」: 「やめてってば！」.

daily.title: Complaining about family to a friend
daily.description: Grumbling that your father keeps telling the same story.
daily.example: Honestly, my dad is telling the same story again.

daily.title: Teasing your partner
daily.description: Answering a partner's joke with playful reproach.
daily.example: Oh, you!

daily.title: Hurrying a child
daily.description: A parent loses patience with a child who won't take a bath.
daily.example: I told you to get in the bath now!

work.title: Private chat with a close coworker
work.description: Lightly complaining about the boss at lunch.
work.example: Our section chief got the meeting time wrong again.

etymology: Usually explained as a contraction of 「〜と言ったら」, originally “speaking of ...”. From marking a topic, it developed emotional tones such as annoyance and affection.

similar.title: 〜（こと）といったら
similar.explanation: 「〜といったら」 brings up a topic and stresses how extreme it is (「寒さといったら」). 「〜ったら」 usually follows a person and shows annoyance or affection.

similar.title: 〜なんて
similar.explanation: 「〜なんて」 looks down on something. 「〜ったら」 has a “what can you do” feeling, often with affection.

similar.title: 〜ってば
similar.explanation: When urging or insisting, it can be swapped with 「〜ったら」, and 「ってば」 is more common. But for bringing up a person as a topic, 「ったら」 is usually used.

title: 〜ということだ (hearsay / conclusion)
meaning: Passes on information you heard (“they say ...”), or draws a conclusion or rephrases what was said (“in other words ...”).
connection: Plain form + ということだ

senses.label: Hearsay
senses.meaning: Passes on information from people, the news, etc.: “they say ...”, “reportedly ...”. More formal and objective than 「そうだ」, and common in news and official notices.
senses.connection: Plain form + ということだ／ということです; often with 「〜によると」 or 「〜の話では」
examples: According to the weather forecast, it will snow tomorrow.
I hear the president is going on an overseas business trip next week.
Reportedly, the cause of the accident is still unknown.

senses.label: Conclusion / rephrasing
senses.meaning: Draws a conclusion from facts or statements, or explains what something really means: “in other words ...”, “that means ...”. Often used with 「つまり」, 「要するに」, or 「〜ということは」.
senses.connection: (つまり／要するに) plain form + ということだ
examples: No reply means it hasn't been decided yet.
So, in other words, this plan is cancelled, right?
In short, it means more practice is needed.

notes: In speech it is often shortened to 「ってことだ」 or 「ってこと」.
「ということは」 often starts a sentence, meaning “so that means ...”, and leads to a conclusion.
As hearsay, it is more objective than 「〜そうだ」. 「〜とのことだ」 is even more formal and often used to pass on messages.

daily.title: Passing on news to family
daily.description: Telling your family about traffic after watching the news.
daily.example: According to the news, the trains will be stopped until evening.

daily.title: Figuring something out
daily.description: Seeing the door locked and guessing with a family member.
daily.example: If the door's locked, that means nobody's home yet.

work.title: Passing on a client's message
work.description: Telling a coworker what the client said.
work.example: According to the client, delivery will be next week.

work.title: Summarizing in a meeting
work.description: Confirming the main point of what someone said.
work.example: So, in other words, we're cutting the budget by 20%, right?

etymology: Made of quoting 「と」 + 「いう」 + the abstract noun 「こと」 + the copula 「だ」. Literally “it is the thing that is said to be ...”. This gave both the hearsay meaning (“someone says ...”) and the rephrasing meaning (“that is to say ...”).

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: Both express hearsay. 「そうだ」 is more common in daily life; 「ということだ」 is more objective and formal, and can also show a conclusion.

similar.title: 〜とのことだ
similar.explanation: 「とのことだ」 is more formal and is often used to pass on someone's message: 「よろしくとのことです」.

similar.title: 〜ということ (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: 「〜ということ」 alone just turns a sentence into a noun (「〜ということが分かった」). Only with 「だ」 as the predicate does it show hearsay or a conclusion.

meaning: Used to define a word or explain its meaning. Also used to bring up something as a topic and comment on it, or at the start of a sentence to give a reason.
connection: Noun／plain form + というのは; sentence-initial: というのは、〜からだ

senses.label: Definition / explanation
senses.meaning: Explains what a word or expression means: “... means ...”, “what we call ... is ...”. Often ends with 「〜のことだ」 or 「〜という意味だ」.
senses.connection: Noun + というのは + 〜のことだ／〜という意味だ
examples: “Halloween” is an autumn festival.
“KY” means someone who can't read the room.
「コンビニ」 means a convenience store.

senses.label: Topic + comment
senses.meaning: Brings up something as a topic, then gives the speaker's opinion or feelings: “..., (that) really is ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form／noun + というのは + comment
examples: Living alone in a foreign country is tough.
Raising children is really difficult.

senses.label: Giving a reason
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence, adds the reason for what was just said, like 「なぜなら」 (“because”). Often ends with 「〜からだ」 or 「〜のだ」.
senses.connection: Sentence-initial: というのは、〜からだ
examples: I can't go tomorrow. That's because my mother is in the hospital.
I'm against this plan, because it costs too much.

notes: In speech, 「〜って」, 「〜っていうのは」, and 「〜ってのは」 are common.
「〜とは」 can also define words with the same meaning, but it is more formal.
For reasons, it is close to 「というのも」, which is a bit more formal.

daily.title: Explaining slang
daily.description: Explaining a young people's word to an older person.
daily.example: “Oshi” means the person you support the most.

daily.title: Sharing a feeling
daily.description: A thought that comes up while chatting with family.
daily.example: Family really is something to be grateful for.

daily.title: Explaining why
daily.description: Telling a friend why you're leaving early today.
daily.example: I'm heading home early today. That's because I have to get up early tomorrow.

work.title: Explaining company jargon
work.description: Explaining a common workplace term to a new employee.
work.example: 「ホウレンソウ」 means reporting, informing, and consulting.

work.title: Giving a reason for a request
work.description: Explaining why you're asking a client for an extension.
work.example: Could you extend the delivery deadline? That's because the parts are arriving late.

etymology: Made of quoting 「と」 + 「いう」 + the nominalizer 「の」 + the topic particle 「は」. Literally “the thing called ...”.

similar.title: 〜とは (definition / surprise)
similar.explanation: For definitions it means the same as 「というのは」. 「とは」 is more formal and common in dictionaries and writing.

similar.title: 〜というのも〜からだ
similar.explanation: Both can start a sentence and give a reason. 「というのも」 is more formal, with a feel of “the reason for this is also ...”.

similar.title: 〜という意味だ
similar.explanation: 「〜という意味だ」 often ends the sentence and pairs with 「〜というのは」 to explain a word's meaning.

meaning: Says that a second description fits better than the first: “rather than ..., it's more like ...”.
connection: Noun／adjective／verb plain form + というより

senses.label: Correcting a description
senses.meaning: First gives one description, then a more accurate one: “it's not so much A as B”. The speaker prefers the second.
senses.connection: Noun／plain form + というより (、B)
examples: He's more like family than a friend.
It's not so much that this room is small; there's just too much stuff.
That's not cooking, it's more like a science experiment.

senses.label: Even stronger degree
senses.meaning: Shows a degree that goes further than the first description: “not just ..., but actually ...”.
senses.connection: Adjective plain form + というより + stronger adjective
examples: Today isn't so much cool as cold.
That story was not so much interesting as moving.

senses.label: With 「むしろ」
senses.meaning: Often used with 「むしろ」 as 「AというよりむしろB」. Clearer, and a bit formal.
senses.connection: 〜というより(も)むしろ〜
examples: This is not so much a failure as a chance for the next step.
Rather than a teacher, he's closer to a friend.

notes: Both descriptions are about the same thing; the speaker thinks the second fits better.
In speech, 「〜っていうか」 and 「〜ってより」 are common.
「AよりB」 compares two different things. 「AというよりB」 picks the better description of one thing.

daily.title: Commenting on food
daily.description: Your reaction to a very spicy curry.
daily.example: This curry isn't so much spicy as painful!

daily.title: Introducing a friend
daily.description: Introducing a very close friend to someone.
daily.example: She's less a friend and more like a sister to me.

daily.title: Talking about a movie
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about a movie you just saw.
daily.example: That movie wasn't so much scary as sad.

work.title: Analyzing a problem
work.description: Pointing out the real issue in a meeting.
work.example: This isn't so much a technical problem as a communication problem.

etymology: Made of quoting 「と」 + 「いう」 + 「より」 (comparison). Literally “rather than calling it ...”.

similar.title: 〜より(も)むしろ
similar.explanation: 「AよりむしろB」 compares two things and chooses B. 「AというよりB」 corrects how one thing is described. They are often combined as 「というよりむしろ」.

similar.title: 〜というか〜というか
similar.explanation: 「というか」 lists several descriptions, meaning it's hard to sum up in one word. 「というより」 clearly picks the second description.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: This compares two different things to say which is better. 「というより」 compares descriptions, not things.
